```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function (arg0_path) {
  lines <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("peru_after_independence.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("peru_after_independence_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

sum_data <- fromJSON("peru_after_independence_summary.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

# Abstract

Peru entered republican independence in 1821 with roughly 1,4M inhabitants scattered across an overwhelmingly highland peasant economy, and over two centuries multiplied twenty-fourfold to reach 34,16M (34.157.732) by 2025 across 26 departmental and metropolitan jurisdictions spanning 1.328.108 km² (15.769 five-arcminute cells). Early republican fiscal registers of 1836, 1850 and 1862 preceded the landmark 1876 national census under President Manuel Pardo, which recorded 2.699.106 residents while revealing coastal plantation expansion fuelled by indentured Chinese labour during the guano boom [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Rodriguez2020Migracion]. Following territorial losses in Tarapacá and Arica during the War of the Pacific (1879-1883) and the eventual 1929 retrocession of Tacna, demographic recovery lifted the republic to 4.686.426 by 1907 and 7.181.683 at the inaugural modern census of 1940, when 65% of Peruvians still inhabited the rural Sierra [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Lujan1966Tasas]. After 1950, rapid mortality decline, agrarian crisis and urban industrialisation triggered a vast highland-to-coast migration known as the *desborde popular*, propelling national totals through 10,60M (1961), 13,81M (1972), 17,76M (1981), 22,05M (1993), 27,41M (2007) and 31,24M (2017) to an estimated 34,07M in 2024 [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Peattle1990Participation; @Mick2010Discursos; @Hernandez2025Lengua]. Concurrently, agricultural colonisation and hydrocarbon extraction accelerated frontier growth across the Amazonian departments of Loreto, San Martín, Ucayali and Madre de Dios, whereas the internal armed conflict of 1980-2000 displaced hundreds of thousands from Ayacucho, Huancavelica and Apurímac [@Broussard2020Sibling; @Cesario2015Migracao]. Integrating historical administrative geometry, pycnophylactic mass-conserving disaggregation and 1.795 geocoded settlements, this study documents how Lima Metropolitana grew from 645.172 residents in 1940 to 10,64M in 2025, concentrating almost one-third of the national population along a narrow desert littoral [@Salazar2021Lima; @Regaladoregalado2020Capital; @Zanella2025Acceso].

# Background

## Independence and Early Republican Fiscal Counts

At the proclamation of independence in July 1821 and the capitulation of royalist forces at Ayacucho in December 1824, Peru inherited the spatial and social architecture of the late Bourbon viceroyalty. Settlement remained anchored in the intermontane basins and high plateaus of the Sierra, where indigenous Quechua and Aymara peasant communities sustained the fiscal base of the early republic [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Hernandez2025Lengua].

Following the temporary abolition of colonial head taxes by José de San Martín, republican treasuries soon restored indigenous capitation under the title *contribución indígena*, pairing it with non-indigenous *contribución de castas* assessments [@Carranza2015Seminario]. Early national population figures therefore derive from provincial tax rolls (*matrículas de contribuyentes*) and electoral censuses compiled in 1836, 1850 and 1862.

Those fiscal registers placed Peru between 1,37M inhabitants in 1836 and 2,49M by 1862 across imperfectly demarcated departments [@Carranza2015Seminario]. Because highland parish registries routinely omitted infants, mobile pastoralists and tax-exempt households, the pre-1876 counts serve as administrative lower bounds rather than uniform demographic enumerations [@Carranza2015Seminario].

City-level counts from 1836 and 1862 confirm a dispersed urban network with low metropolitan primacy. Lima held 55.627 inhabitants in 1836, 94.195 in 1857 and 100.341 in 1862, while Cusco declined slightly from 20.371 in 1836 to 18.370 in 1862 after losing southern colonial commercial circuits [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Rendon2024Expansion].

## The Landmark 1876 National Census under Manuel Pardo

The structural watershed in nineteenth-century Peruvian statistics arrived with the national census of 14 May 1876, ordered by President Manuel Pardo and directed by Manuel Atanasio Fuentes at the newly founded Dirección de Estadística. Enumerating 2.699.106 inhabitants across departments and littoral provinces, the 1876 census remains the foundational baseline for modern Andean demographic history [@Carranza2015Seminario].

Its territorial breakdown revealed that three-quarters of Peruvians still lived in the highlands. Ancash (284.091), Puno (256.594), Cusco (238.445), Cajamarca (213.391) and Junín (209.871) dwarfed coastal jurisdictions outside the central Lima-Callao corridor [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Gavilano2017Mineria].

Urban concentrations remained modest even in departmental capitals. Lima contained 101.488 residents inside its old municipal perimeter, Callao numbered 34.492, Arequipa 29.237, Cusco 18.370, Tacna 14.183 and Chiclayo 11.325, while northern Amazonian Iquitos was still a river village of 1.475 people [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Cesario2015Migracao].

## Guano Wealth and Coastal Asian Immigration

Between 1845 and 1876, Chincha Islands guano exports transformed state revenues and financed railway construction alongside irrigated sugar and cotton estates along the northern and central desert valleys. When President Ramón Castilla abolished both the *contribución indígena* and African slavery in 1854, coastal estate owners faced acute seasonal and permanent labour shortages [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Rodriguez2020Migracion].

Planters and state contractors filled that deficit through the Pacific coolie trade, importing roughly 90k to 100k indentured Chinese workers (*culíes*) from Guangdong via Macao between 1849 and 1874 [@Rodriguez2020Migracion]. Concentrated in the sugar valleys of La Libertad, Lambayeque and Lima as well as coastal cities, Chinese migrants and their descendants reshaped coastal urban commerce and formed Lima's enduring Asian-Peruvian community [@Rodriguez2020Migracion; @Chen2016Technology].

Following diplomatic restrictions on indentured Chinese contracts, bilateral treaties opened a second trans-Pacific stream in 1899 with the arrival of contracted Japanese labourers. Japanese families settled initially on coastal haciendas in Chancay, Cañete and Lima before establishing urban small-business networks across Lima and Callao [@Rodriguez2020Migracion].

## The War of the Pacific and Southern Boundary Shifts

Guano-funded coastal expansion collapsed abruptly during the War of the Pacific (1879-1883). Following Chilean occupation of Lima and southern coastal ports, the 1883 Treaty of Ancón permanently ceded the nitrate-rich southern department of Tarapacá to Chile and placed the provinces of Tacna and Arica under temporary Chilean administration pending a delayed plebiscite [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Accinelli2017Imitation].

Over four decades of diplomatic deadlock, Peruvian migration and commerce in the far south remained disrupted until the 1929 Treaty of Lima partitioned the contested zone. Chile retained Arica permanently while retroceding Tacna to Peruvian sovereignty, leaving Tacna's 1940 departmental population at just 37.512 compared with 50.449 estimated in 1907 [@Accinelli2017Imitation].

Within the post-1883 borders, demographic recovery accelerated during the *República Aristocrática* (1895-1919). Copper mining and railway links in Cerro de Pasco and Junín, northern coastal sugar consolidation and the Amazonian rubber boom around Iquitos lifted national population to 4.686.426 in the 1907 sub-prefectural compilation [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Gavilano2017Mineria; @Cesario2015Migracao].

## The 1940 Census Baseline and the Post-1950 Desborde Popular

Sixty-four years elapsed without a national enumeration until President Manuel Prado's administration conducted the census of June 1940 [@Lujan1966Tasas]. Recording 7.181.683 inhabitants across the republic, the 1940 baseline documented a country still overwhelmingly rural and highland: roughly 65% of Peruvians inhabited rural districts, and the Sierra held the clear demographic majority [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Hernandez2025Lengua].

Even so, early metropolitan concentration was already evident. Lima Metropolitana had expanded to 645.172 residents in 1940 (including 520.528 in Lima city proper and 82.287 in Callao), while Piura (431.487) and La Libertad (404.024) gained weight relative to stagnant southern Andean departments [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Salazar2021Lima].

After 1950, declining infectious-disease and infant mortality drove natural population growth above 2,5% annually while highland agriculture stagnated under population pressure and fragmented *minifundios* [@Broussard2020Sibling; @Lujan1966Tasas]. Millions of Quechua, Aymara and mestizo migrants descended along newly paved trans-Andean highways from Ancash, Ayacucho, Apurímac, Cajamarca, Huancavelica and Puno toward coastal cities in the transformation termed the *desborde popular* [@Rodriguez2020Migracion; @Mick2010Discursos; @Hernandez2025Lengua].

Because formal housing markets excluded low-income provincial arrivals, migrant families organised collective land occupations (*barriadas*, later named *pueblos jóvenes* and *asentamientos humanos*) across desert hills and river fans north, east and south of Lima [@Peattle1990Participation; @Valladolid2015Arquitectura; @Zanella2025Acceso]. National headcounts climbed from 10.602.283 in 1961 to 13.813.779 in 1972 and 17.762.231 in 1981, while Lima Metropolitana grew nearly threefold from 1,85M to 4,57M over those two decades [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Peattle1990Participation; @Valladolid2015Arquitectura].

Along the central and northern littoral, secondary industrial and fishing ports absorbed parallel migration streams. Chimbote expanded from a village of 4.243 people in 1940 to 216.579 in 1981 through steelworks and anchoveta fishmeal processing, while Trujillo, Chiclayo, Piura and Arequipa multiplied severalfold [@Alvitres2014Influencia; @Gavilano2017Mineria].

## Amazonian Colonisation, Internal Conflict and Modern Transitions

East of the Andes, demographic expansion shifted from the early twentieth-century wild rubber boom in Iquitos toward state-promoted agricultural colonisation after 1960. Opening of the *Carretera Marginal de la Selva* and hydrocarbon exploration drew highland smallholders from Cajamarca, Amazonas, Huánuco and Cusco into San Martín, Ucayali and Madre de Dios [@Cesario2015Migracao].

Between 1940 and 2025, San Martín grew eightfold from 120.913 to 967.923 inhabitants and Madre de Dios expanded more than eightfold from 25.212 to 208.667, driven by alluvial gold extraction, timber and road integration toward Acre in western Brazil [@Cesario2015Migracao]. Ucayali likewise rose from 112.749 in 1940 to 623.868 by 2025 around its river port of Pucallpa (Callería) [@Cesario2015Migracao].

Between 1980 and 2000, internal armed conflict waged by Sendero Luminoso and counterinsurgency forces inflicted severe demographic dislocation across the south-central highlands [@Broussard2020Sibling]. Ayacucho suffered an absolute inter-censal decline from 523.821 inhabitants in 1981 to 492.507 in 1993, and Pasco fell from 229.701 to 226.295, while tens of thousands fled Huancavelica and Apurímac for Lima, Huancayo and coastal Ica [@Broussard2020Sibling; @Haller2018Urbanization].

Macroeconomic hyperinflation in the late 1980s simultaneously launched mass international emigration (*El Quinto Suyo*) to the United States, Spain, Argentina, Chile and Japan, placing over three million Peruvians abroad by the 2010s [@Munoz2005Nota; @Caycho2013Paerregaard; @Baiadera2016Berg; @Fantagarrido2019Migracion]. After 2000, rapid fertility decline and expanded public health insurance (*Seguro Integral de Salud*) reduced under-one mortality across both rural and urban cohorts [@Espinolasanchez2025Impact; @Broussard2020Sibling].

Between 2017 and 2022, Peru's migration balance reversed as over one million Venezuelans entered coastal cities, concentrating heavily in Lima, Callao, Trujillo and Arequipa [@Sacristanrodriguez2022Migracion; @Arroyolaguna2023Migration]. Although the 2020-2022 SARS-CoV-2 pandemic caused one of the sharpest adult mortality surges recorded globally, INEI benchmarks show continued recovery from 31.237.385 in 2017 to 34.068.276 in 2024 and 34.157.732 in 2025 [@Silva2024Using; @Salazar2021Lima].

# Methodology

## Sub-Administrative Geometry and Post-1876 Benchmarks

Reconstructing Peruvian population surfaces across two centuries requires harmonising shifting republican boundaries with modern departmental units. For the pre-1883 horizon, OpenHistoricalMap and historical administrative polygons preserve Peru's sovereign jurisdiction over Tarapacá and the undivided southern littoral prior to the Treaty of Ancón [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Gavilano2017Mineria].

Post-1883 regimes transition cleanly through historical 1890, 1920, 1950, 1970, 2000, 2010 and 2025 departmental geometries across 407 recorded sub-administrative units [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Gavilano2017Mineria]. Inside the modern national domain, Peru is partitioned into 26 territorial units comprising the 24 historical departments plus the Constitutional Province of El Callao (546 km²) and the Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima (3.429 km²), while retaining the surrounding nine provinces of Lima Region (33.299 km²) as a separate departmental polygon.

Total domain area across the 5-arcminute raster mask equals 1.328.108 km² (15.769 active cells), closely matching the 1.332.701 km² summed from smoothed vector departmental polygons. Benchmark enumerations anchor ten primary intervals (1876, 1907, 1940, 1961, 1972, 1981, 1993, 2007, 2017 and 2025), supplemented by the 2024 official projection (34.068.276) and pre-1876 fiscal counts (1836, 1850 and 1862) for major urban nodes [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Lujan1966Tasas].

For 1907, where newly created San Martín (separated from Loreto in September 1906) lacked a disaggregated departmental total in the primary compilation, the raw benchmark retains a placeholder floor of 1 while Loreto carries the undivided upper Amazonian tally of 100.596. Confidence envelopes around departmental benchmarks widen from plus or minus 2,5% in post-1961 modern censuses to plus or minus 6% in 1876, 1907 and 1940 enumerations [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Lujan1966Tasas].

## Spatial Allocation, Kriging Substrata and Municipal Consolidation

To disaggregate departmental census totals onto 5-arcminute grid cells without artificial border cliffs, this study combines biophysical suitability covariates with Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging calibrated across the broader Andean-Southern Cone domain [@Haller2018Urbanization; @Miloslavich2025Percepcion]. That substratum draws on 1.599 active domestic catchments out of 2.238 total catchments, incorporating 101.856 primary heritage and archaeological site records with a median Voronoi radius of 27,84 km and zero crowd-sourced fallback.

Within each historical snapshot year, pycnophylactic mass-conserving disaggregation enforces exact agreement between raster cell sums and departmental enumeration totals:

$$P_{d}(t) = \sum_{c \in \Omega_d} \hat{w}_c(t) \, \frac{T_d(t)}{\sum_{j \in \Omega_d} \hat{w}_j(t)}$$

where $T_d(t)$ denotes the enumerated population of department $d$ at benchmark $t$, $\Omega_d$ is the set of 5-arcminute pixels assigned to $d$, and $\hat{w}_c(t)$ is the composite dasymetric weight blending kriged settlement substrata, fluvial proximity, coastal access and urban mask buffers [@Rendon2024Expansion; @Gavilano2017Mineria].

Urban settlement accounting applies strict anti-double-counting rules across metropolitan boundaries [@Salazar2021Lima; @Regaladoregalado2020Capital]. The 43 constituent districts of Lima Province are consolidated into one unified capital city entity, Lima (9.600.043 in 2025), rather than splitting historic Cercado de Lima from populous peripheral districts such as San Juan de Lurigancho, Ate, Villa El Salvador or Comas [@Valladolid2015Arquitectura; @Zanella2025Acceso].

Conversely, the 7 districts of the Constitutional Province of Callao are consolidated into Callao (1.043.538 in 2025) and tagged as an extra-municipal port suburb outside Lima's municipal jurisdiction, while Lima Metropolitana (10.643.581 in 2025, peaking at 11,17M in 2022) represents their joint metropolitan envelope [@Salazar2021Lima; @Lujan1966Tasas]. Because the central coordinates of Lima and Callao fall inside the shared coastal pixel cluster along the Callao-Lima frontier, both Lima and Lima Metropolitana snap spatially to the El Callao 5-arcminute cell group alongside Callao, whereas Ricardo Palma falls inside the eastern perimeter of the Lima Metropolitan mask polygon.

# Testing and Validation

Validation across the Peruvian dataset rests on three independent checks: mass-conservation fidelity across historical boundary transitions, source-ledger saturation across the settlement gazetteer, and cross-validation against modern departmental demographic surveys [@Silva2024Using; @Espinolasanchez2025Impact].

Pycnophylactic mass-conservation audits confirm maximum relative error below $4,9 \times 10^{-8}$ across every active sub-administrative unit from 1800 through 2025. That precision guarantees zero population leakage when departments split (such as Tumbes, Pasco in 1944, or Ucayali in 1980) or when southern borders shifted after 1883 and 1929 [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Accinelli2017Imitation].

Across the settlement gazetteer, four sequential ingestion waves evaluated 1.846 candidate district and historical urban entries from national census registers, retaining 1.795 included settlements and excluding 51 candidate entries (34 duplicate historical aliases and 17 unlocated or recently created district toponyms lacking georeferenced coordinates in the primary national gazetteer).

Wave-over-wave marginal gain declined monotonically from 100% (1.432 entries in Wave 1) to 17,53% (251 repairs in Wave 2), 6,36% (107 nineteenth- and twentieth-century longitudinal backfills in Wave 3) and 0,28% (5 gap-hunter additions in Wave 4), reaching full asymptotic saturation with 0% crowd-sourced fallback. Every one of the 26 sub-regional mask polygons contains active settlements, ranging from 163 entries in Ancash, 129 in Cajamarca and 127 in Lima Region to 10 in Madre de Dios and 3 consolidated municipal or metropolitan entries in El Callao [@Miloslavich2025Percepcion; @Gavilano2017Mineria].

# Results

## National Trajectory and the Great Coastal Shift

Peru's aggregate demographic history after independence divides into three distinct growth regimes, visible in Figure \ref{fig:peru-trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:peru-dept-early}. During the first regime (1876-1940), population expanded at an annual compound rate of 1,52%, rising from 2.699.106 in 1876 to 4.686.426 in 1907 and 7.181.683 in 1940 [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Lujan1966Tasas]. Despite steady recovery from the War of the Pacific, high rural infant mortality and recurrent epidemics restrained natural increase, keeping national density below 5,4 inhabitants per km² in 1940 [@Broussard2020Sibling; @Carranza2015Seminario].

During the second regime (1940-1981), public health campaigns, malaria eradication along coastal valleys and antibiotics halved mortality while birth rates remained elevated, accelerating annual growth to 2,23% across four decades [@Broussard2020Sibling; @Lujan1966Tasas]. National population more than doubled from 7,18M in 1940 to 17,76M in 1981, while the spatial centre of gravity lurched decisively westward toward the Pacific [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Peattle1990Participation].

Lima Metropolitana surged from 611.403 in 1940 (inside the provincial boundary) to 1.695.682 in 1961, 2.997.453 in 1972 and 4.443.798 in 1981, while adjacent Callao grew over fivefold from 84.438 to 454.313 [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Valladolid2015Arquitectura]. Rapid expansion radiated outward along three urban axes: the northern cone toward Comas and Independencia, the eastern Rimac axis toward San Juan de Lurigancho and Ate, and the southern desert settlements of Villa María del Triunfo and Villa El Salvador [@Peattle1990Participation; @Valladolid2015Arquitectura; @Regaladoregalado2020Capital; @Zanella2025Acceso].

Northern coastal departments recorded parallel industrial and agro-export expansion over the same decades. La Libertad climbed from 404.024 in 1940 to 1.011.631 in 1981, Lambayeque from 199.660 to 708.820, and Piura from 431.487 to 1.155.682, despite periodic El Niño flooding disruptions along northern littoral plains [@Alvitres2014Influencia; @Gavilano2017Mineria]. In Ancash, the catastrophic 1970 Yungay-Huaraz earthquake accelerated highland out-migration toward coastal Chimbote, which reached 216.579 residents by 1981 before Nuevo Chimbote emerged as an adjacent urban district [@Gavilano2017Mineria].

During the third regime (1981-2025), sustained fertility decline cooled national growth to 1,50% per year even as absolute population nearly doubled from 17,76M to 34,16M [@Espinolasanchez2025Impact; @Silva2024Using]. By 2025, the Lima-Callao conurbation alone housed 11,24M inhabitants across the metropolitan province and Callao (representing 32,9% of Peru), achieving an urban density of 2.809 inhabitants per km² in Lima Metropolitana and 1.447 per km² in Callao (Figure \ref{fig:peru-trajectory}B) [@Salazar2021Lima; @Regaladoregalado2020Capital; @Chen2016Technology].

Meanwhile, high-altitude southern Sierra departments stalled or contracted relative to the nation. Huancavelica stood at 372.158 in 2025 (below its 2007 peak of 454.797), Pasco fell to 253.549 (below its 2007 count of 280.449), and Puno plateaued near 1,23M amid persistent rural out-migration and lakeside ecological pressures around Lake Titicaca [@Broussard2020Sibling; @Tumiquispe2024Preocupaciones].

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/peru_after_independence_population_trajectory.png",
  "Departmental demographic trajectories (1876-2025) and leading regional population densities in 2025 across Peru.",
  "fig:peru-trajectory"
)
```

```{r tab-dept-early, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
dept_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (arg0_rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[arg0_rk]]
  p <- r$population
  nm <- r$name
  if (identical(nm, "Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima")) nm <- "Lima Metropolitana (Prov.)"
  if (identical(nm, "Lima")) nm <- "Lima (Region)"
  data.frame(
    Department = nm,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(r$area_km2, 0L),
    Y1876 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1876"]]),
    Y1907 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1907"]]),
    Y1940 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1940"]]),
    Y1961 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1961"]]),
    Y1981 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1981"]]),
    Y2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2025"]]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
dept_df <- do.call(rbind, dept_rows)
rownames(dept_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  dept_df,
  "Departmental area and population across Peru at primary census benchmarks from 1876 to 2025 (n=26 territorial units).",
  c("Department", "Area (km²)", "1876", "1907", "1940", "1961", "1981", "2025"),
  list(label = "tab:peru-dept-early", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 30L)
)
```

## Urban Hierarchy, Regional Primacy and Rank-Size Structure

Figure \ref{fig:peru-hierarchy} contrasts Peru's primate urban hierarchy against the Zipfian rank-size profile of all 1.795 catalogued settlements. Lima Metropolitana dominates the national system at 11,17M (2022 metropolitan peak; 10,64M in 2025), followed by the unified Lima municipal core at 9,60M, Arequipa at 1,13M (2022 urban agglomeration), Callao at 1,04M, and Trujillo at 1,03M [@Salazar2021Lima; @Chen2016Technology; @Zanella2025Acceso]. Below the million-resident threshold, a secondary tier of coastal agro-commercial ports, highland regional capitals and Amazonian river hubs anchors regional administration: Chiclayo (663,2k), Piura (547,1k), Cusco (492,4k), Huancayo (450,9k), Iquitos (430,7k), Chimbote (395,1k), Tacna (334k), Ica (325,7k) and Juliaca (316,9k) [@Haller2018Urbanization; @Rendon2024Expansion; @Gavilano2017Mineria].

In the upper tail above 25k residents, the settlement rank-size distribution fits a classic Zipf power law with slope $\alpha = 1$ and $R^2 = 0,98$, yet two clear structural breaks appear at opposite ends of the curve (Figure \ref{fig:peru-hierarchy}B). At rank 1 and 2, Lima Metropolitana and unified Lima sit markedly above the fitted line, reflecting three centuries of administrative, fiscal and transport centralisation amplified by post-1950 coastal migration [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Peattle1990Participation; @Salazar2021Lima]. Below rank 200 (roughly 20k inhabitants), the curve bends sharply downward as hundreds of small rural Andean and Amazonian district capitals drop off rapidly in size across fragmented mountain topography [@Rendon2024Expansion; @Miloslavich2025Percepcion].

```{r fig-hierarchy, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/peru_after_independence_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Peak population of leading Peruvian settlements and the national settlement rank-size distribution (1.795 catalogued centres).",
  "fig:peru-hierarchy"
)
```

## Regional Divergence: Coast, Sierra and Selva

Grouping the 26 territorial units by natural macro-region highlights the scale of Peru's spatial transformation between 1876 and 2025 (Table \ref{tab:peru-macro-regions}). The coastal belt (Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad, Lima Metropolitana, Callao, Lima Region, Ica, Moquegua and Tacna) rose from 22,3% of national population in 1876 (602.501) to 30,8% in 1940 (2,21M) and 58,2% by 2025 (19,88M).

Coastal urbanisation rested on Lima's manufacturing and service economy alongside commercial cotton, sugar and asparagus irrigation in Ica (growing seventeenfold from 60.111 in 1876 to 1,03M in 2025) and Lambayeque (rising sixteenfold from 85.984 to 1,40M) [@Alvitres2014Influencia; @Accinelli2017Imitation]. Tacna similarly rebounded from 37.512 in 1940 after treaty retrocession to 389.226 in 2025 through cross-border trade with northern Chile [@Accinelli2017Imitation].

Across the Sierra (Ancash, Apurímac, Arequipa, Ayacucho, Cajamarca, Cusco, Huancavelica, Huánuco, Junín, Pasco and Puno), demographic growth lagged steadily behind national rates after 1940 despite high initial fertility [@Broussard2020Sibling]. These eleven Andean departments collectively held 72,6% of Peruvians in 1876 (1,96M) and 60,0% in 1940 (4,31M), yet dropped to 32,1% by 2025 (10,97M) [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Hernandez2025Lengua].

Within the highlands, population redistributed internally from dispersed agrarian villages into departmental commercial nodes such as Arequipa, Huancayo, Cusco, Cajamarca, Juliaca and Huamachuco, encroaching on surrounding valley pastures and mountain conservation zones [@Haller2018Urbanization; @Miloslavich2025Percepcion; @Gavilano2017Mineria; @Rendon2024Expansion]. Meanwhile, the Amazonian Selva (Amazonas, Loreto, Madre de Dios, San Martín and Ucayali) expanded its national share from 5,1% in 1876 (136.253) to 9,7% in 2025 (3,30M), led by Loreto (1,03M), San Martín (967.923) and Ucayali (623.868) [@Cesario2015Migracao].

```{r tab-macro-regions, results='asis'}
coast_ids <- c(
  "per_tumbes", "per_piura", "per_lambayeque", "per_la_libertad",
  "per_municipalidad_metropolitana_de_lima", "per_el_callao", "per_lima",
  "per_ica", "per_moquegua", "per_tacna"
)
sierra_ids <- c(
  "per_ancash", "per_apurimac", "per_arequipa", "per_ayacucho",
  "per_cajamarca", "per_cusco", "per_huancavelica", "per_huanuco",
  "per_junin", "per_pasco", "per_puno"
)
selva_ids <- c(
  "per_amazonas", "per_loreto", "per_madre_de_dios",
  "per_san_martin", "per_ucayali"
)

sum_zone <- function (arg0_ids, arg1_yr) {
  sum(vapply(arg0_ids, function (arg0_id) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[arg0_id]]$population[[arg1_yr]]), numeric(1)))
}
sum_area <- function (arg0_ids) {
  sum(vapply(arg0_ids, function (arg0_id) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[arg0_id]]$area_km2), numeric(1)))
}

zones <- list(
  list(label = "Costa (10 littoral units)", ids = coast_ids),
  list(label = "Sierra (11 Andean departments)", ids = sierra_ids),
  list(label = "Selva (5 Amazonian departments)", ids = selva_ids)
)
tot_2025 <- sum_zone(names(mod_data$regions), "2025")

macro_rows <- lapply(zones, function (arg0_z) {
  p1876 <- sum_zone(arg0_z$ids, "1876")
  p1940 <- sum_zone(arg0_z$ids, "1940")
  p1981 <- sum_zone(arg0_z$ids, "1981")
  p2025 <- sum_zone(arg0_z$ids, "2025")
  a_km2 <- sum_area(arg0_z$ids)
  data.frame(
    Zone = arg0_z$label,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(a_km2, 0L),
    Y1876 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1876),
    Y1940 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1940),
    Y1981 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1981),
    Y2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(p2025),
    Share2025 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * p2025 / tot_2025, 1L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
macro_df <- do.call(rbind, macro_rows)
rownames(macro_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  macro_df,
  "Macro-regional redistribution of Peruvian population across Costa, Sierra and Selva groupings (1876-2025).",
  c("Macro-Region", "Area (km²)", "1876", "1940", "1981", "2025", "2025 Share"),
  list(label = "tab:peru-macro-regions", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

# Limitations

Four empirical constraints bear on the interpretation of these historical series. First, pre-1940 population figures combine uneven fiscal registers (1836-1862), the 1876 census (which faced accessibility barriers in remote Amazonian basins and non-Spanish-speaking highland parishes) and 1907 sub-prefectural compilations lacking disaggregated returns for newly created San Martín [@Carranza2015Seminario].

Second, War of the Pacific territorial losses require careful boundary continuity. Tarapacá and Arica enter pre-1883 historical polygons under Peruvian administration and transition thereafter out of the republican frame, while Tacna's 1907 and 1940 series reflect occupation and post-retrocession recovery [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Accinelli2017Imitation].

Third, sub-metropolitan district boundaries complicate city-level comparisons in secondary cities. While Lima (43 districts) and Callao (7 districts) are cleanly consolidated in the settlement gazetteer, provincial capitals such as Arequipa, Trujillo, Chiclayo, Piura, Cusco and Huancayo blend multi-district urban agglomeration series for 1940-1993 and 2022 with individual central-district counts in the 2007, 2017 and 2025 census extracts [@Haller2018Urbanization; @Rendon2024Expansion]. In Arequipa, for example, the central district stood at 52.930 in 2025 while neighbouring Cerro Colorado reached 262.059 and the wider urban agglomeration exceeded 1,13M.

Fourth, recent 2020-2025 dynamics remain sensitive to excess pandemic mortality and unrecorded circular cross-border flows of Venezuelan migrants and Peruvian emigrants [@Silva2024Using; @Sacristanrodriguez2022Migracion; @Caycho2013Paerregaard; @Arroyolaguna2023Migration].

# Conclusion

Over the two centuries following independence, Peru inverted an ancient Andean demographic equilibrium. Throughout the colonial era and the first republican century, the highland Sierra sustained the dense agrarian majority while the arid coast hosted thin irrigated oases and a modest administrative port network [@Carranza2015Seminario; @Hernandez2025Lengua].

Between 1940 and 2025, mortality decline, highland agrarian crisis, highway integration and two decades of internal conflict triggered mass migration toward the Pacific littoral and eastern Amazonian valleys [@Lujan1966Tasas; @Peattle1990Participation; @Broussard2020Sibling; @Cesario2015Migracao]. Nationally, Peru expanded from 2,70M in 1876 to 7,18M in 1940 and 34,16M in 2025, while Lima Metropolitana grew more than sixteenfold over the last 85 years to become one of the foremost urban agglomerations of the Americas [@Salazar2021Lima; @Regaladoregalado2020Capital; @Zanella2025Acceso].

By reconciling historical administrative boundaries, kriged settlement substrata and 1.795 geocoded district and urban centres, this synthesis establishes a consistent demographic baseline for studying modern Andean urbanisation and regional divergence.

# Appendix

Table \ref{tab:peru-dept-late} provides the complementary mid-to-late twentieth- and twenty-first-century census benchmarks (1972, 1993, 2007, 2017 and 2024) alongside 2025 departmental population densities for all 26 territorial units of Peru.

Whereas the 2024 column reports official INEI departmental projections summing to 34.068.276, the 2025 column integrates census-calibrated municipal and provincial district updates summing to 34.157.732.

In Table \ref{tab:peru-dept-early}, the 1907 entry for San Martín (1) marks its 1906 administrative separation from Loreto prior to independent sub-prefectural tabulation; combined upper Amazonian totals for that benchmark reside in Loreto (100.596).

```{r tab-dept-late, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
late_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (arg0_rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[arg0_rk]]
  p <- r$population
  nm <- r$name
  if (identical(nm, "Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima")) nm <- "Lima Metropolitana (Prov.)"
  if (identical(nm, "Lima")) nm <- "Lima (Region)"
  dens <- as.numeric(p[["2025"]]) / as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  data.frame(
    Department = nm,
    Y1972 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1972"]]),
    Y1993 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1993"]]),
    Y2007 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2007"]]),
    Y2017 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2017"]]),
    Y2024 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2024"]]),
    Dens2025 = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 1L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
late_df <- do.call(rbind, late_rows)
rownames(late_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  late_df,
  "Complementary Peruvian departmental census benchmarks (1972-2024) and 2025 population density (inhabitants per km²).",
  c("Department", "1972", "1993", "2007", "2017", "2024", "2025 Density"),
  list(label = "tab:peru-dept-late", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 30L)
)
```
